Q78. Create a class Distance with a parameterized constructor that adds two distance objects (feet and inches).

Unit II CO2 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

Object arithmetic with physical unit conversion (12 inches = 1 foot):

class Distance {
    int feet;
    int inches;

    Distance(int f, int i) {
        this.feet = f + (i / 12);
        this.inches = i % 12;
    }

    // Method to add another Distance object
    Distance add(Distance d2) {
        int totalInches = this.inches + d2.inches;
        int totalFeet = this.feet + d2.feet + (totalInches / 12);
        int finalInches = totalInches % 12;
        return new Distance(totalFeet, finalInches);
    }

    void display() {
        System.out.println(feet + " ft " + inches + " in");
    }
}

public class DistanceDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Distance d1 = new Distance(5, 9);
        Distance d2 = new Distance(3, 7);
        Distance sum = d1.add(d2);
        System.out.print("Total Distance: ");
        sum.display(); // 9 ft 4 in (9+7=16 in = 1 ft 4 in)
    }
}

Quick Recall: Add feet and inches separately, carrying over 1 foot for every 12 inches ($12\text{ in} = 1\text{ ft}$).

🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
Distance class Object passing Unit conversion Constructor initialization

Q141. Write a program that displays a message when the mouse enters and exits a component.

Unit IV CO4 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

The MouseListener interface captures pointer transitions across component bounding boxes via the mouseEntered() and mouseExited() callbacks.

Program Implementation

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class MouseBoundaryMonitor extends Frame implements MouseListener {
    private Panel sensorBox;
    private Label lblStatus;

    public MouseBoundaryMonitor() {
        setTitle("Mouse Boundary Monitor");
        setLayout(new BorderLayout(10, 10));

        sensorBox = new Panel();
        sensorBox.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Slate background

        lblStatus = new Label("Status: Hover your mouse inside the dark box above", Label.CENTER);

        // Register listener with the target sensor panel
        sensorBox.addMouseListener(this);

        add(sensorBox, BorderLayout.CENTER);
        add(lblStatus, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            @Override
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        setSize(440, 260);
        setLocationRelativeTo(null);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    @Override
    public void mouseEntered(MouseEvent e) {
        sensorBox.setBackground(new Color(56, 189, 248)); // Sky blue highlight
        lblStatus.setText("Status: Mouse has ENTERED the panel boundary! (" + e.getX() + ", " + e.getY() + ")");
    }

    @Override
    public void mouseExited(MouseEvent e) {
        sensorBox.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Restore slate
        lblStatus.setText("Status: Mouse has EXITED the panel boundary.");
    }

    // Required MouseListener methods satisfied with empty bodies
    public void mouseClicked(MouseEvent e) {}
    public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) {}
    public void mouseReleased(MouseEvent e) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new MouseBoundaryMonitor();
    }
}

Technical Analysis

  • Boundary Crossing: mouseEntered triggers immediately when the hardware cursor intersects the component's visible bounding rect. mouseExited triggers when it moves outside.
  • Coordinate Data: e.getX() and e.getY() provide the component-relative pixel position of the cursor upon entry.
  • Interface Contract: All 5 methods of MouseListener must be present, or developers can subclass MouseAdapter to override only desired methods.
  • Expected Interaction Behavior: Hovering the cursor inside the dark panel instantly turns the background sky blue and prints the coordinates. Moving the pointer out restores the dark slate color and updates the footer label.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • MouseListener listens for what the mouse is doing over a component.
  • mouseEntered fires as soon as the mouse hovers inside our box (we light it up).
  • mouseExited fires the exact instant the mouse leaves the box.
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
MouseListener mouseEntered mouseExited MouseEvent Panel WindowAdapter

Q145. Write a basic Applet example that displays a message in paint() and identify where init() is used.

Unit IV CO4 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

An Applet is an embeddable Java GUI component designed to execute within an external browser environment or the Applet Viewer utility.

Applet Code Implementation

import java.applet.Applet;
import java.awt.Graphics;
import java.awt.Color;
import java.awt.Font;

/*
<applet code="HelloApplet.class" width="400" height="180">
</applet>
*/
public class HelloApplet extends Applet {
    private String bannerText;

    // init() is invoked ONCE when the applet is first instantiated
    @Override
    public void init() {
        setBackground(new Color(15, 23, 42)); // Dark slate background
        bannerText = "Welcome to Java Applet Architecture!";
        System.out.println("init() lifecycle hook executed: State initialized.");
    }

    // paint() is called whenever the screen canvas needs repainting
    @Override
    public void paint(Graphics g) {
        g.setColor(new Color(56, 189, 248)); // Cyan text
        g.setFont(new Font("SansSerif", Font.BOLD, 18));
        g.drawString(bannerText, 30, 90);
    }
}

The Role and Purpose of init()

  • First Lifecycle Milestone: The init() method is the first method called by the browser runtime immediately after the applet class bytecode is loaded into memory.
  • Initialization Tasks: It functions as the applet's conceptual constructor. Developers use it to parse HTML <param> tags, load fonts and images, create child AWT components, and set background/foreground palettes.
  • Execution Frequency: Unlike start() and paint() which can execute multiple times whenever a browser tab is revisited or resized, init() is strictly guaranteed to execute only once per applet session.
  • Lifecycle Transitions: The complete sequence is init() → start() → paint(). If the user navigates away or minimizes the browser, stop() pauses the applet. When the browser tab is closed, destroy() releases resources.

Because applets inherit from java.awt.Panel, they support nested layouts, event listeners, and graphics rendering using double buffering to avoid screen flicker.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • An Applet is a mini Java application that runs inside an old-school browser or viewer.
  • init() runs first and only once: it's where you setup variables, fonts, and background colors.
  • paint(Graphics g) draws the visual shapes and text onto the screen using g.drawString().
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
Applet init() paint() Graphics drawString Applet Lifecycle

Q146. [IMAGE Q6: Show a window containing a text field, a button labelled Show, and an output label.] Analyze the interface and write the event-handling code for the Show button.

Unit IV CO4 | Bloom L4 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

Interface Architectural Analysis:

The GUI comprises three visual tiers managed under an event-driven lifecycle:

  • Input Layer: A TextField designated for user keyboard entry.
  • Trigger Layer: A push Button labeled "Show" which registers an ActionListener and functions as the event generator.
  • Presentation Layer: An output Label serving as the passive display sink to reflect the processed text.

Under the Java Delegation Event Model, clicking "Show" generates an ActionEvent. The runtime pushes this event onto the Event Dispatch Thread (EDT), routing it to actionPerformed().

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class ShowTextApp extends Frame implements ActionListener {
    private TextField txtInput;
    private Button btnShow;
    private Label lblOutput;

    public ShowTextApp() {
        setTitle("Show Text Interface");
        setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 15, 15));

        // Instantiate components
        txtInput = new TextField(20);
        btnShow = new Button("Show");
        lblOutput = new Label("Awaiting input...", Label.CENTER);

        // Register event listener with the event source
        btnShow.addActionListener(this);

        // Assemble GUI hierarchy
        add(new Label("Enter Text:"));
        add(txtInput);
        add(btnShow);
        add(lblOutput);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        setSize(360, 160);
        setLocationRelativeTo(null);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    // Event-handling callback logic
    @Override
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        String input = txtInput.getText().trim();
        if (input.isEmpty()) {
            lblOutput.setText("Notice: Please enter some text first!");
        } else {
            lblOutput.setText("Displayed Content: " + input);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new ShowTextApp();
    }
}

Execution Trace & User Feedback Pipeline

When the user enters "Java GUI Programming" into the text field and triggers the "Show" button, the Event Dispatch Thread reads the input buffer via txtInput.getText(), wraps it in the formatted label string, and immediately invalidates the label peer to repaint the new text cleanly.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • Anatomy: A text box + a "Show" button + a text label below.
  • How It Works: You type your text into the box. When you press "Show", Java calls actionPerformed.
  • The Transfer: The code grabs the text via txtInput.getText() and instantly transfers it into lblOutput.setText(...).

The program below registers a MouseListener on a specialized canvas/panel to capture and report mouse cursor interactions:

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class PanelMouseTracker extends Frame implements MouseListener {
    private Panel sensorPanel;
    private Label lblFeedback;

    public PanelMouseTracker() {
        setTitle("Panel Mouse Interaction Tracker");
        setLayout(new BorderLayout(8, 8));

        sensorPanel = new Panel();
        sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Slate background

        lblFeedback = new Label("Move mouse over the box or click inside it", Label.CENTER);

        // Attach MouseListener to the sub-container
        sensorPanel.addMouseListener(this);

        add(sensorPanel, BorderLayout.CENTER);
        add(lblFeedback, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        setSize(420, 260);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    @Override
    public void mouseClicked(MouseEvent e) {
        sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(52, 211, 153)); // Green on click
        lblFeedback.setText("Mouse CLICKED at (" + e.getX() + ", " + e.getY() + ")! Click count: " + e.getClickCount());
    }

    @Override
    public void mouseEntered(MouseEvent e) {
        sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(56, 189, 248)); // Blue on enter
        lblFeedback.setText("Mouse ENTERED the panel area.");
    }

    @Override
    public void mouseExited(MouseEvent e) {
        sensorPanel.setBackground(new Color(30, 41, 59)); // Restore slate
        lblFeedback.setText("Mouse EXITED the panel area.");
    }

    // Unused methods satisfied for interface contract
    public void mousePressed(MouseEvent e) {}
    public void mouseReleased(MouseEvent e) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new PanelMouseTracker();
    }
}

Interaction Lifecycle & Coordinate Feedback

Moving the mouse cursor over the dark sensor panel triggers mouseEntered(), turning the panel background bright blue. Moving outside triggers mouseExited(), restoring the dark background. Clicking inside the panel invokes mouseClicked(), which retrieves precise coordinates via e.getX() and e.getY() and flashes the panel green.

The MouseEvent object also provides e.getClickCount() to distinguish between single-clicks and double-clicks, and e.getButton() to identify left versus right mouse button clicks.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • Attaches a MouseListener to an interactive panel box.
  • Entering turns the box blue; exiting resets it back to slate; clicking turns it green and reports the exact $(X, Y)$ coordinate!

Q167. Name two states in the life cycle of a thread.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L1 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

The Java thread lifecycle (defined in Thread.State) includes six distinct states. Two core states are:

  1. NEW: A thread is in this initial state after instantiation (new Thread()) but before the start() method has been invoked. No OS call stack has been allocated yet.
  2. RUNNABLE: After start() is invoked, the thread enters the RUNNABLE state. It is either executing instructions on a CPU core or waiting in the operating system ready queue for processor scheduling.

Other states include: BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and TERMINATED.

State transitions occur dynamically: invoking sleep() or wait() shifts a thread from RUNNABLE to TIMED_WAITING or WAITING. When the timer expires or notify() is called, the thread returns to RUNNABLE.

Quick Revision:

  • NEW: Thread object is born in memory, but not yet started.
  • RUNNABLE: Thread is actively running on the CPU or ready and waiting for its CPU time slice.
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
NEW state RUNNABLE state Thread.State Thread Lifecycle start()

Q177. Explain when a finally block is executed.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L2 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

In Java, a finally block is guaranteed to execute under virtually all circumstances, regardless of whether an exception is thrown or caught within the preceding try and catch blocks.

Execution Rules:

  • Normal Flow: Executes immediately after the try block completes without errors.
  • Handled Exception: Executes immediately after the matching catch block completes.
  • Unhandled Exception: Executes before the uncaught exception propagates up the call stack to abort the thread.
  • Return Statements: Even if try or catch executes a return, break, or continue statement, the finally block executes before the return actually resolves!

Sole Exception: The only scenario where finally does not execute is if the JVM terminates abruptly via System.exit(0) or an OS-level fatal kill.

Quick Revision:

  • The finally block always runs—rain or shine, error or no error, even if there is a return statement.
  • Used for essential cleanup: closing open files, network sockets, or database connections.
  • The only thing that stops it is calling System.exit(0).
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
finally block always executes resource cleanup System.exit return statement

Q180. Create two threads using the Runnable interface and start them.

The code below demonstrates creating and launching two independent concurrent threads using the Runnable interface:

class TaskWorker implements Runnable {
    private String taskName;

    public TaskWorker(String name) {
        this.taskName = name;
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++) {
            System.out.println(taskName + " executing step " + i);
        }
    }
}

public class TwoThreadsRunnableDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // 1. Create Runnable task instances
        Runnable task1 = new TaskWorker("Task-Alpha");
        Runnable task2 = new TaskWorker("Task-Beta");

        // 2. Wrap tasks in Thread objects
        Thread t1 = new Thread(task1);
        Thread t2 = new Thread(task2);

        // 3. Launch both threads concurrently
        t1.start();
        t2.start();
    }
}

By passing distinct Runnable instances (or the same instance) into new Thread(task), both threads execute concurrently on separate call stacks, sharing CPU timeslices without blocking the main application thread.

Using Runnable promotes clean architecture by separating the executable business task from the underlying system thread resource allocation, enabling seamless integration with Java thread pools like Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2).

  • Pass your runnable object into new Thread(task).

Q191. Write a program to create a thread by implementing Runnable. Print five numbers from the run() method.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

Implementing the Runnable interface represents the industry-standard architectural pattern for multithreading in Java, establishing a clean separation between task execution logic and JVM thread lifecycle management.

Program Implementation

// 1. Define task logic by implementing Runnable
class NumberSequenceTask implements Runnable {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println("Worker thread initiated: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
            System.out.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] Sequence Number: " + i);
            try {
                // Brief pause to simulate computational work
                Thread.sleep(300);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.err.println("Thread interrupted: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Worker thread finished: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }
}

public class RunnableThreadDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Main thread starting execution...");

        // 2. Instantiate the task target
        NumberSequenceTask task = new NumberSequenceTask();

        // 3. Wrap task inside Thread instance and assign descriptive name
        Thread workerThread = new Thread(task, "NumberWorker-1");

        // 4. Initiate thread execution via start()
        workerThread.start();

        System.out.println("Main thread continues independent operations...");
    }
}

Architectural Highlights & Execution Flow

  • Separation of Concerns: Runnable encapsulates the computational unit of work (the "what"), while Thread manages OS thread allocation and scheduling (the "how").
  • Single Inheritance Preservation: Because Java disallows multiple class inheritance, implementing Runnable preserves the class's ability to extend other domain bases (e.g. extends JPanel implements Runnable).
  • Execution Lifecycle: Calling workerThread.start() creates a new native OS call stack, transitions the thread into the RUNNABLE state, and asynchronously invokes run() to print numbers 1 through 5.
  • Thread Pool Compatibility: Runnable instances can be directly submitted to modern Java concurrency utilities such as ExecutorService.

Detailed Step-by-Step Program Walkthrough

1. Implementing Runnable: The class NumberSequenceTask implements the functional interface Runnable by providing the concrete implementation of its single abstract method run().

2. Thread Construction: In main(), an instance of NumberSequenceTask is passed to the Thread(Runnable target, String name) constructor. This associates the execution logic with the newly created thread.

3. Thread Execution Lifecycle: Calling workerThread.start() signals the JVM to request a new operating system thread, initialize a dedicated call stack, and call run() asynchronously. Inside run(), the for-loop executes five iterations, pausing for 300ms between numbers using Thread.sleep().

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • We create a task by writing implements Runnable and putting a 1-to-5 loop inside run().
  • In main(), we hand that task to a new Thread worker and call start().
  • The worker prints numbers 1 to 5 with nice brief pauses while the main program keeps rolling.
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
Runnable Thread start() run() Thread.sleep NumberSequenceTask

Q194. Write a program that handles NumberFormatException when converting user input into an integer.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.2

The program below demonstrates robust conversion of string input into numeric integer primitives using Integer.parseInt() while guarding against malformed inputs via NumberFormatException:

import java.util.Scanner;

public class NumberFormatSafeParser {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
        String[] testInputs = {"42", "3.1415", "one-hundred", "99999"};

        for (String rawInput : testInputs) {
            System.out.println("
Evaluating input string: "" + rawInput + """);
            try {
                // Parsing attempt (throws NumberFormatException if non-integer characters exist)
                int parsedValue = Integer.parseInt(rawInput.trim());
                int square = parsedValue * parsedValue;
                System.out.println("Success! Parsed integer: " + parsedValue + " (Square: " + square + ")");
            } catch (NumberFormatException nfe) {
                System.err.println("NumberFormatException Caught: Cannot parse "" + rawInput + "" into an integer.");
                System.err.println("Diagnostic Reason: " + nfe.getMessage());
            } finally {
                System.out.println("Finished parsing cycle for: "" + rawInput + """);
            }
        }
        scanner.close();
    }
}

Root Cause: NumberFormatException is an unchecked exception (subclass of IllegalArgumentException) thrown when a string contains invalid radix characters, decimal points, or values outside the 32-bit signed integer range ($-2^{31}$ to $2^{31}-1$).

Radix Parsing Mechanics & Boundary Validation

Integer.parseInt(s) validates that the string consists solely of an optional ASCII sign (+ or -) followed by decimal digits. If the input contains letters, decimal points (e.g. "3.14"), spaces, or values exceeding signed 32-bit limits ($[-2^{31}, 2^{31}-1]$), it throws NumberFormatException, ensuring corrupt data never enters the domain model.

In real-world applications, input parsing is wrapped in loop validation so users are prompted repeatedly until they supply a clean, valid integer.

Proper exception handling prevents application crashes and provides clear diagnostics to end users.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • When you ask Java to convert words like "hello" or "3.14" into a whole integer via Integer.parseInt(), Java throws a NumberFormatException.
  • Wrapping the parse call in try-catch catches the bad input and prints an error instead of crashing the program!
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
NumberFormatException Integer.parseInt() try-catch IllegalArgumentException input sanitization

    }

        new HobbySelector();
    }
}

Technical Highlights & Event Mechanics

  • Non-Exclusive Selection: Unlike radio buttons, standalone Checkbox instances allow users to choose none, either, or both hobbies concurrently.
  • ItemListener Interface: Handles state change notifications via itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e) whenever a box is toggled.
  • State Inspection: Calling cb.getState() returns a primitive boolean (true if selected, false if unselected).
  • Dynamic String Construction: StringBuilder efficiently aggregates active selections without producing unnecessary intermediate String garbage on the heap.
  • Expected Execution Behavior: When the user checks 'Reading Books', the status label updates to 'Selected: Reading Books; '. Toggling 'Outdoor Sports' appends it. Unchecking both resets the label to 'Selected: None'.

  • Whenever a box is checked or unchecked, Java fires an ItemEvent.
  • The method cb.getState() checks if the box is checked, and we update the message on screen.

Program Implementation

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class FeedbackForm extends Frame implements ActionListener {
    private TextArea taFeedback;
    private Button btnSubmit;
    private Label lblConfirm;

    public FeedbackForm() {
        setTitle("Student Feedback System");
        setLayout(new BorderLayout(10, 10));

        Label lblHeader = new Label("Please enter your detailed feedback below:", Label.CENTER);
        
        // TextArea configured with 6 rows, 35 columns, and vertical scrollbars
        taFeedback = new TextArea("", 6, 35, TextArea.SCROLLBARS_VERTICAL_ONLY);
        
        Panel southPanel = new Panel(new FlowLayout());
        btnSubmit = new Button("Submit Feedback");
        lblConfirm = new Label("Awaiting user submission...");
        
        btnSubmit.addActionListener(this);
        southPanel.add(btnSubmit);
        southPanel.add(lblConfirm);

        add(lblHeader, BorderLayout.NORTH);
        add(taFeedback, BorderLayout.CENTER);
        add(southPanel, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            @Override
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        pack(); // Sizes window to fit preferred component dimensions
        setLocationRelativeTo(null);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    @Override
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        String feedback = taFeedback.getText().trim();
        if (feedback.isEmpty()) {
            lblConfirm.setForeground(Color.RED);
            lblConfirm.setText("Error: Feedback cannot be blank!");
        } else {
            lblConfirm.setForeground(new Color(16, 185, 129));
            lblConfirm.setText("Thank you! Feedback recorded (" + feedback.length() + " chars).");

import java.awt.*;

public class SemesterSelector extends Frame implements ItemListener {

        rbSem5 = new Checkbox("Semester V (Autumn)", semGroup, false);

        lblSelected = new Label("Current Selection: Semester IV (Spring)", Label.CENTER);

Q174. Describe one advantage of implementing Runnable.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L2 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.1

The primary advantage of implementing the Runnable interface over extending the Thread class is overcoming Java's single inheritance limitation.

Because Java does not permit multiple class inheritance, a class that extends Thread cannot inherit from any other class. By implementing Runnable, your worker class preserves its single inheritance slot, enabling it to inherit from other domain classes or framework bases (such as extends Applet or extends JFrame):

// Can inherit from Frame AND execute as a concurrent thread
public class GameWindow extends Frame implements Runnable {
    public void run() {
        // Game loop animation logic
    }
}

Additionally, it decouples task definition from thread execution mechanism, allowing use with modern thread pools (ExecutorService).

Quick Revision:

  • Java only allows extending one parent class.
  • If you extend Thread, you can't extend anything else.
  • By implementing Runnable, your class can still extend whatever class it needs (e.g., extends JPanel implements Runnable).
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
Runnable single inheritance Thread extension separation of concerns ExecutorService

Q178. Describe one difference between ArrayList and HashSet.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L2 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.1

The primary architectural difference between ArrayList and HashSet lies in their element uniqueness and ordering guarantees:

Dimension java.util.ArrayList java.util.HashSet
Interface & Duplicates Implements List. Allows duplicate elements freely. Implements Set. Disallows duplicate elements; duplicate insertions are rejected.
Ordering Maintains strict insertion order based on 0-based integer indices. Unordered; makes no guarantees about element iteration sequence.
Underlying Data Structure Dynamic resizable object array. Internal hash table (backed by a HashMap instance). 
List list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("A", "A", "B")); // Size: 3 (duplicates retained)
Set set = new HashSet<>(List.of("A", "A", "B"));    // Size: 2 (duplicate "A" filtered)

Quick Revision:

  • ArrayList keeps the exact order you put items in and happily allows duplicate values.
  • HashSet is like a unique mathematical bag: it scrambles the order but guarantees that every item is unique!
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
ArrayList vs HashSet List vs Set duplicate elements insertion order hash table

Q181. Use sleep() in a thread program to pause execution briefly between messages.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L3 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.1

The program below utilizes Thread.sleep() to introduce a 1000-millisecond delay between sequential console messages, properly catching InterruptedException:

public class SleepDemoThread extends Thread {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        String[] alerts = {"System Initializing...", "Connecting to Server...", "Ready for Commands."};
        for (String msg : alerts) {
            System.out.println(msg);
            try {
                // Pause current thread for 1000 milliseconds (1 second)
                Thread.sleep(1000);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.err.println("Thread sleep was interrupted: " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new SleepDemoThread().start();
    }
}

Thread.sleep() places the calling thread in the TIMED_WAITING state while maintaining all acquired synchronization locks.

If another active thread invokes interrupt() on the sleeping thread, Thread.sleep() immediately terminates the sleep interval, clears the interrupt status, and throws InterruptedException for graceful handling.

Quick Revision:

  • Thread.sleep(1000) pauses the thread for 1 second.
  • You must wrap it in a try-catch block for InterruptedException because another thread could wake it up early.
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
Thread.sleep InterruptedException TIMED_WAITING pause execution try-catch

Q193. Create a program with two threads that print their names and demonstrate the use of setName() and getName().

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.1

Assigning descriptive, readable names to concurrent threads is essential for multi-threaded debugging, production logging, and thread dump inspection. The program below demonstrates naming threads using setName() and querying identities via getName().

Program Implementation

class NamedWorkerThread extends Thread {
    public NamedWorkerThread(String initialName) {
        super(initialName);
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        // Query active thread identity inside the execution loop
        System.out.println("run() executing on thread -> " + getName());
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            System.out.println("[" + getName() + "] Processing computational batch #" + i);
            try {
                Thread.sleep(250);
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                System.err.println("[" + getName() + "] Interrupted!");
            }
        }
        System.out.println("[" + getName() + "] Task finished.");
    }
}

public class ThreadNamingDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Instantiate two threads with default names
        NamedWorkerThread t1 = new NamedWorkerThread("Default-1");
        NamedWorkerThread t2 = new NamedWorkerThread("Default-2");

        System.out.println("Original Name of T1: " + t1.getName());
        System.out.println("Original Name of T2: " + t2.getName());

        // Explicitly reassign descriptive operational names
        t1.setName("DatabaseSync-Thread");
        t2.setName("FileExport-Thread");

        System.out.println("Updated Name of T1: " + t1.getName());
        System.out.println("Updated Name of T2: " + t2.getName());

        // Launch concurrent execution
        t1.start();
        t2.start();
    }
}

Technical Significance & Diagnostics

  • Default Naming: When names are omitted, the JVM assigns sequential generic names such as Thread-0, Thread-1, which obscure error sources in production logs.
  • Runtime Mutability: setName(String name) can be invoked before or during thread execution, allowing threads to update their names to reflect active processing tasks.
  • Thread Dumps & Profilers: In enterprise diagnostics (via jstack or VisualVM), custom names allow administrators to instantly pinpoint blocked, deadlocked, or resource-heavy worker threads.

Step-by-Step Execution Walkthrough

1. Default Naming: When threads are instantiated without explicit names, the JVM assigns automatic identifiers (such as Thread-0 and Thread-1). Calling getName() reads this value.

2. Renaming Threads: The method t1.setName("DatabaseSync-Thread") modifies the thread's internal name string attribute. This can be called at any point during thread existence.

3. Diagnostic Logging: Inside run(), printing getName() confirms that each concurrent worker prints its custom descriptive name during each batch iteration, ensuring full traceability in application log files.

Additionally, Thread.currentThread().getId() returns the positive long integer assigned as the unique thread identifier for the lifetime of the JVM thread.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • By default, Java names threads boring names like "Thread-0".
  • We use t1.setName("DatabaseSync-Thread") to give them real, descriptive nametags.
  • Inside the thread, calling getName() prints the nametag so your console logs are crystal clear!
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
setName() getName() Thread thread naming debugging NamedWorkerThread

Q139. Write a program with a choice/ComboBox containing three course names.

Unit IV CO4 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.0

The java.awt.Choice class implements a compact, space-efficient drop-down selection menu (analogous to Swing's JComboBox) where a user selects one item from a list.

Program Implementation

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class ChoiceDropdownDemo extends Frame implements ItemListener {
    private Choice courseChoice;
    private Label lblSelected;

    public ChoiceDropdownDemo() {
        setTitle("AWT Choice Component Demo");
        setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 20, 20));

        Label lblPrompt = new Label("Select Academic Subject:");
        courseChoice = new Choice();

        // Populate drop-down options
        courseChoice.add("Design and Analysis of Algorithms");
        courseChoice.add("Object Oriented Programming with Java");
        courseChoice.add("Relational Database Management Systems");

        lblSelected = new Label("Selected: " + courseChoice.getSelectedItem());

        // Register listener for selection changes
        courseChoice.addItemListener(this);

        add(lblPrompt);
        add(courseChoice);
        add(lblSelected);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            @Override
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        setSize(440, 180);
        setLocationRelativeTo(null);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    @Override
    public void itemStateChanged(ItemEvent e) {
        lblSelected.setText("Selected: " + courseChoice.getSelectedItem() + 
                            " (Index " + courseChoice.getSelectedIndex() + ")");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new ChoiceDropdownDemo();
    }
}

Technical Details & Method Capabilities

  • Population: Elements are appended using choice.add(String item) or choice.insert(String item, int index).
  • Selection Retrieval: getSelectedItem() returns the chosen string, while getSelectedIndex() returns its 0-based integer index.
  • Event Dispatch: Selecting a different element emits an ItemEvent, which is routed to itemStateChanged().
  • Screen Real Estate: Unlike a List, a Choice remains collapsed until clicked, occupying minimal UI space.
  • Additional Utility Methods: getItemCount() returns total items (3), remove(String item) deletes an entry, and select(int index) sets the programmatically highlighted default.
  • Expected Behavior: Clicking the choice drops down all three subjects. Selecting any item updates the label with its full title and index.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • Choice is AWT's pop-up drop-down menu.
  • You add options with choice.add("Course Name").
  • When a student selects an option, courseChoice.getSelectedItem() tells you what was chosen.

Choice getSelectedItem ItemListener java.awt.Choice drop-down menu

Q143. Write a program that displays a message dialog when a user clicks a button.

Unit IV CO4 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.0

In Java AWT, modal alert popups are created using the java.awt.Dialog class. The program below launches a modal dialog upon clicking an alert button.

Program Implementation

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class DialogDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener {
    private Button btnLaunch;

    public DialogDemo() {
        setTitle("AWT Dialog System");
        setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 25, 25));

        btnLaunch = new Button("Launch Information Dialog");
        btnLaunch.addActionListener(this);
        add(btnLaunch);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            @Override
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        setSize(360, 160);
        setLocationRelativeTo(null);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    @Override
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        // Construct modal dialog: parent Frame, Title, boolean modal
        Dialog infoDialog = new Dialog(this, "Alert Notification", true);
        infoDialog.setLayout(new FlowLayout(FlowLayout.CENTER, 15, 15));

        Label lblMessage = new Label("System Alert: Operation completed successfully!");
        Button btnDismiss = new Button("Acknowledge & Close");

        btnDismiss.addActionListener(ae -> infoDialog.setVisible(false));

        infoDialog.add(lblMessage);
        infoDialog.add(btnDismiss);
        infoDialog.setSize(300, 140);
        infoDialog.setLocationRelativeTo(this);
        infoDialog.setVisible(true); // Blocks until dismissed due to modality
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new DialogDemo();
    }
}

Modal vs Modeless Architecture

  • Modal Dialogs: Passing true as the third argument constructs a modal dialog, preventing user interaction with all parent windows until closed.
  • Event Blocking: The call infoDialog.setVisible(true) blocks further thread progression on that call stack until setVisible(false) or dispose() is invoked.
  • Resource Disposal: Dismissing a dialog with dispose() frees native OS window handles.
  • Modality Comparison: Passing false creates a modeless dialog where users can freely click back and forth between the popup and the parent window.
  • Expected Execution Behavior: Clicking the launch button opens a compact 300x140 popup window centered on the main frame. The parent frame remains unresponsive until 'Acknowledge & Close' is pressed.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • A Dialog is a pop-up sub-window that alerts the user.
  • Setting modal = true freezes the main window so the user must click "OK" before doing anything else.
  • Calling dialog.setVisible(false) dismisses the alert.
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
Dialog modal dialog Message Dialog ActionListener Frame setLocationRelativeTo

Q155. Create a GUI with a TextArea and a Clear button. Clear the text area when the button is clicked.

Unit IV CO4 | Bloom L3 5 Marks End Term Score: 9.0

The application below provides a multi-line note editor featuring a reset/clear mechanism that blanks the TextArea and returns focus:

import java.awt.*;
import java.awt.event.*;

public class TextEditorClearDemo extends Frame implements ActionListener {
    private TextArea textArea;
    private Button btnClear;
    private Label lblCharCount;

    public TextEditorClearDemo() {
        setTitle("Scratchpad & Text Reset Utility");
        setLayout(new BorderLayout(8, 8));

        textArea = new TextArea("Type initial notes here...
Line 2
Line 3", 8, 30);
        btnClear = new Button("Clear All Text");
        lblCharCount = new Label("Characters: 43");

        btnClear.addActionListener(this);

        Panel bottomPanel = new Panel(new FlowLayout());
        bottomPanel.add(btnClear);
        bottomPanel.add(lblCharCount);

        add(new Label("Enter your notes below:", Label.CENTER), BorderLayout.NORTH);
        add(textArea, BorderLayout.CENTER);
        add(bottomPanel, BorderLayout.SOUTH);

        addWindowListener(new WindowAdapter() {
            public void windowClosing(WindowEvent e) {
                System.exit(0);
            }
        });

        pack();
        setLocationRelativeTo(null);
        setVisible(true);
    }

    @Override
    public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
        // Reset text area content to empty string
        textArea.setText("");
        lblCharCount.setText("Characters: 0 (Cleared!)");
        // Return keyboard focus to the text area for immediate typing
        textArea.requestFocus();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new TextEditorClearDemo();
    }
}

Technical Detail: Calling textArea.setText("") clears both displayed characters and internal buffer, while requestFocus() provides superior UX by positioning the blinking cursor back inside the editor.

Buffer Management & Cursor Positioning

A TextArea maintains an internal character buffer. Invoking textArea.setText("") clears all lines of text and resets the scrollbars to top position. Calling textArea.requestFocus() immediately directs hardware keyboard focus back to the editor, ensuring the user can begin typing immediately without clicking.

In real-world text editors, the clear operation is often paired with an 'Undo' buffer or a confirmation dialog to prevent accidental data loss when resetting extensive notes.

This ensures seamless and responsive interaction during long editing sessions.

ELI5 Breakdown:

  • Creates a multi-line notebook area with a "Clear All Text" button below.
  • Clicking the button calls textArea.setText("") which wipes the notepad clean.
  • requestFocus() pops the blinking cursor right back inside so you can start typing again immediately.

Q169. Name the purpose of try and catch blocks.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L2 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.0

The try and catch blocks form Java's core mechanism for robust runtime exception handling:

  • try Block Purpose: Encloses a section of "guarded" statements that might generate an abnormal condition or throw an exception during execution. If an exception occurs, the remaining statements in the try block are skipped.
  • catch Block Purpose: Immediately follows the try block to intercept, identify, and handle the thrown exception object. It prevents abrupt JVM program termination and executes recovery or logging logic.
try {
    int quotient = 100 / 0; // Risky code
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Caught and handled: " + e.getMessage()); // Graceful recovery
}

Quick Revision:

  • try is the safety net where you wrap risky operations.
  • catch catches the error if something blows up, preventing the application from crashing.
🎯 Evaluator Scoring Keywords:
try block catch block guarded region graceful recovery ArithmeticException

Q179. Write a short program that creates a thread by extending Thread and prints three messages.

Unit V CO5 | Bloom L3 3 Marks End Term Score: 9.0

The program below demonstrates thread creation by subclassing Thread, overriding run(), and invoking start() to execute three messages:

// Custom thread subclass
class MessagePrinterThread extends Thread {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            System.out.println("Thread Message #" + i + " from " + getName());
        }
    }
}

public class ThreadSubclassDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Instantiate and initiate thread execution
        MessagePrinterThread worker = new MessagePrinterThread();
        worker.setName("Worker-Thread");
        worker.start(); // Spawns thread and invokes run()
    }
}

Calling worker.start() creates the independent execution thread which runs the loop printing three messages asynchronously.

Subclassing Thread binds the execution logic directly to the thread object. Calling worker.start() creates the native call stack, transitions the thread to RUNNABLE, and asynchronously executes the three output statements.

The method Thread.currentThread() returns a reference to the actively running thread, allowing inspecting thread state, group, and alive status via isAlive().

Quick Revision:

  • Create a class that extends Thread.
  • Put your code inside public void run() with a loop printing 3 times.
  • In main(), call worker.start() to run it concurrently.

extends Thread run() start() getName() MessagePrinterThread

Q183. Use ArrayList to add, remove, and display three city names.

The following code demonstrates core manipulation methods (add, remove, and iteration) using java.util.ArrayList:

import java.util.ArrayList;

public class CityArrayListDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // Instantiate a generic ArrayList of Strings
        ArrayList cities = new ArrayList<>();

        // 1. Add three city names
        cities.add("Mumbai");
        cities.add("Bengaluru");
        cities.add("New Delhi");
        System.out.println("Initial List: " + cities);

        // 2. Remove one city (by value or index)
        cities.remove("Mumbai");
        System.out.println("After removing Mumbai: " + cities);

        // 3. Display remaining cities using an enhanced for-loop
        System.out.println("Displaying remaining cities:");
        for (String city : cities) {
            System.out.println(" - " + city);
        }
    }
}

Calling cities.remove("Mumbai") shifts subsequent elements left to close the gap, maintaining contiguous storage in $O(n)$ time while preserving the insertion order of Bengaluru and New Delhi.
